class.name: LightCatcher3D
class.brief_description: Measures how brightly the scene's lights light a point, so gameplay can react to light and shadow.
class.description:
[LightCatcher3D] measures how brightly lit its [member sample_points] are, the way the renderer lights them: the same energy, colour, range, attenuation and spot cone as [OmniLight3D], [SpotLight3D], [DirectionalLight3D] and [AreaLight3D] draw with, physical light units, [member Light3D.light_projector] cookies and distance fade included. Walls block light, either through physics raycasts against [member occlusion_mask] or, with [member occlusion_source], through the meshes that cast shadows on screen. Put one on a player and enemies can tell whether the player is standing in the light, caught in a flashlight's beam, or hiding in the dark; put one on a stealth pickup, a plant that grows towards light, or a vampire. The [signal light_entered] and [signal light_exited] signals say when a particular light, such as a flashlight, lands on it or leaves. [codeblock] # On an enemy: see the player only where they're lit. @export var player_light: LightCatcher3D
func can_see_player() -> bool: return has_line_of_sight() and player_light.is_lit() [/codeblock] Brightness is in the units diffuse shading uses: a white surface facing a light of energy [code]1.0[/code] at full strength reads [code]1.0[/code], and its colour on screen is its albedo times this, before exposure and tonemapping. The environment's ambient light and global illumination aren't counted, only lights. A flashlight's cookie shapes what it lights, as on screen: its dark ring and dark spots light nothing. As in the renderer, a cookie only applies to a light with [member Light3D.shadow_enabled] on, and an [OmniLight3D]'s cookie is a panorama. The cookie is read at full resolution, where the renderer may blur it with mipmaps far away, so the two can differ right at a cookie's edges. Lights fading out with distance ([member Light3D.distance_fade_enabled]) fade by their distance from the current camera, as they do on screen. To find where a flashlight's beam lands, so an enemy can investigate a lit spot while the player stays out of sight, raycast along the light and measure the hit with its normal: [codeblock] var hit := get_world_3d().direct_space_state.intersect_ray( PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D.create(flashlight.global_position, flashlight.global_position - flashlight.global_basis.z * flashlight.spot_range)) if hit and catcher.measure_point(hit.position, hit.normal) > catcher.threshold: investigate(hit.position) [/codeblock] It updates on physics frames. In the editor it updates a few times a second, so its gizmo shows how lit each sample point is while you place lights: dark grey in shadow, bright yellow at [member threshold], with a line to each light that reaches it when selected.

method.name: get_brightest_light
method.description: Returns the light that gave the most light at the last update, or [code]null[/code] in the dark.

method.name: get_brightness
method.description: Returns how brightly lit the sample points were at the last update, as luminance, combined as [member combine] says and smoothed by [member response_time]. Negative lights can bring it down, but never below [code]0.0[/code].

method.name: get_light_color
method.description: Returns the colour of the light at the last update, in linear units, so a red lamp gives a red colour. Its luminance is [method get_brightness] before smoothing.

method.name: get_light_contribution
method.description: Returns how much [param light] gave at the last update, combined over the sample points as [member combine] says. [code]0.0[/code] if it didn't reach.

method.name: get_lights
method.description: Returns every light that reached a sample point at the last update.

method.name: get_point_brightness
method.description: Returns how brightly the sample point at index [param point] was lit at the last update, before smoothing.

method.name: is_lit
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] while [method get_brightness] is at or above [member threshold]. Once lit, it stays lit until the brightness falls under 80% of the threshold, so a light flickering around the threshold doesn't toggle it every frame.

method.name: measure_point
method.description: Measures how brightly the lights light [param global_position] right now, with this node's settings, without changing what it caught. With a [param normal], the point is a surface facing that way, lit less by light arriving at a slant; without, it faces each light. Use it to ask about places rather than this node: is the spot a noise came from lit, is a hiding place dark?

method.name: measure_point_color
method.description: Like [method measure_point], but returns the light's colour in linear units.

method.name: update_now
method.description: Measures right away instead of waiting for the next physics frame, and emits any signals that follows.

members.member: If [code]false[/code], it stops measuring and keeps what it last caught.
How the sample points' brightness becomes one: the brightest of them, or their average.
How far towards a [DirectionalLight3D] the occlusion ray looks for something blocking it.

If [code]true[/code], the [CollisionObject3D]s this node is inside, such as the player's own body, don't block light. Collision objects a light is inside, such as a lamp's fitting, never block that light.
Only lights on these render layers ([member VisualInstance3D.layers]) count, so lights that are only for looks can be left out.
Whether walls block light. See [enum Occlusion].

How far short of a light the occlusion ray stops, so the light's own lamp shade or bulb mesh doesn't count as blocking it. Rays also leave from just off the measured point, so a point on a surface, such as where a beam lands on a wall, isn't shadowed by that surface.
The physics layers that block light, when [member occlusion_source] uses colliders.
What blocks light: collision shapes, the meshes that cast shadows on screen, or both. See [enum OcclusionSource].
How many seconds [method get_brightness] takes to follow a change, roughly. [code]0.0[/code] follows at once; a little smooths over flicker and lets eyes "adjust".
The points it measures at, in this node's space. A few spread over a character, such as head, chest and feet, catch light falling on any part of them.
The brightness at which it counts as lit, and at which a single light counts as having reached it for [signal light_entered].
Seconds between measurements. [code]0.0[/code] measures every physics frame; a larger value saves raycasts for catchers that don't need to react at once.

signal.name: light_entered
signal.description: Emitted when [param light] alone starts giving at least [member threshold]: a flashlight beam landing, a lamp walked under.

signal.name: light_exited
signal.description: Emitted when [param light] stops giving at least [member threshold], or goes away.

constants.constant: The brightest sample point counts: any part of a character in the light shows them.
The average of the sample points: how much of a character is lit.
Walls block every light, whether it casts shadows or not, which is what players expect of a light behind a wall.
Walls only block lights with [member Light3D.shadow_enabled], dimmed by their [member Light3D.shadow_opacity], matching what's drawn: a light without shadows shines through walls on screen too.
Nothing blocks light, and no raycasts are made.
Physics raycasts against [member occlusion_mask]. Cheap, but a wall needs collision to block light, and an invisible collider blocks light the screen shows passing.

The meshes the renderer draws into each light's shadow: visible [GeometryInstance3D]s that cast shadows, on the light's [member Light3D.shadow_caster_mask]. Agrees with the shadows on screen, at the cost of testing triangles; [MeshInstance3D], [MultiMeshInstance3D] and CSG shapes count. The catcher's own body's meshes don't shadow it when [member exclude_parent_bodies] is on.
